question: A Grade IIIB open tibial fracture arrives at 11 PM. Theatre is busy and will not be free until 7 AM the next day (8 hours later). The registrar says 'we have missed the 6-hour window — infection is inevitable.' Which statement best reflects current evidence?

answers.text: The 6-hour rule is absolute; any delay beyond 6 hours doubles the infection rate.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The strict 6-hour rule is not supported by Level I evidence. BOAST guidelines have moved away from it; what matters is antibiotics within 1 hour and debridement as soon as possible.

answers.text: Antibiotics within 1 hour and debridement within 24 hours is acceptable for most Grade III fractures without vascular compromise.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Current guidelines prioritise early antibiotics over arbitrary time-to-theatre windows. Grade IIIC (vascular) needs emergency theatre, but IIIB without vascular injury can safely await the next available team.

answers.text: Debridement can be safely deferred to 48 hours if antibiotics are given.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: 48 hours is excessive. While the 6-hour rule is not absolute, debridement should happen as early as practically possible and ideally within 24 hours.

answers.text: Grade IIIB always requires emergency vascular surgery within 6 hours.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Grade IIIB has extensive soft-tissue loss but an intact vascular supply. Emergency vascular surgery is required for Grade IIIC (arterial injury).

overallFeedback.feedback: The 6-hour rule has been superseded. Antibiotics within 1 hour is the hard standard; theatre timing for IIIB (no vascular injury) is 'next available within 24 hours'.
Good. Antibiotics in 1 hour, debridement as soon as practically possible (within 24 h for non-vascular). IIIC = vascular emergency.
